title: Huawei bid to build Egypt’s AI data centres, and Washington is scrambling
content:
Huawei has bid to build AI data centres for the Egyptian government. The US State Department is now trying to assemble a rival consortium from Nvidia, AMD and Microsoft.
The tender offer proposes exporting 1,408 of Huawei’s top-end Ascend 950-series chips for an AI training cloud. A further 600, either the same chips or the older 910B, would run two inference clusters. Huawei set out a 12-month build.
Mackenzie Hawkins reported the bid for Bloomberg, from people familiar with the matter and documents she reviewed. Gao Yuan and Matt Day contributed.
It would be the first Ascend export anyone has confirmed
Huawei has spent more than a year trying to sell these chips abroad without a completed deal. Last year it approached buyers in the Gulf and Southeast Asia with a couple of thousand processors. It offered only its second-best model, because production of the better 910C was too low.
This time it is offering the 950DT, which sits above the 910C. Huawei touted those chips at an event in South Korea last year, and the head of its Latin American cloud business told the South China Morning Post it is studying whether to sell them there too.
Huawei declined to comment. Egypt’s foreign ministry did not respond to Bloomberg’s questions.
The volume is small and that is part of the point
The full order comes to 2,008 chips. Under typical training parameters that is roughly the capability of a few hundred top Nvidia processors, orders of magnitude below what Western companies deploy routinely.
For Huawei, a completed sale would prove two things at once: that foreign demand exists, and that it can now supply. US restrictions on chipmaking tools have held its volumes down for years.
Small first shipments into non-traditional markets are also the playbook that made Huawei the world’s largest telecoms equipment supplier.
iFlytek is in the bid, and so is a police ministry logo
The proposal is a partnership with iFlytek, the Chinese speech and surveillance company. Both firms have been on a US blacklist since 2019.
Their joint offering includes vehicle and individual recognition, run against a national population database. It also covers what the documents call situation awareness, packaged as a “one screen panoramic view of the city”.
The presentation runs to 102 pages. On one slide, the examples given for “basic video applications” carry the insignia of China’s Ministry of Public Security.
iFlytek did not respond. Bloomberg reports it is unclear what the American proposal would offer, or whether Washington would restrict any uses of the technology it supplied.
Washington’s response is a consortium and a warning
When the Trump administration learned of the pitch, the State Department contacted Nvidia, AMD and Microsoft about a counter-bid. Microsoft declined to comment and the other two did not respond.
“Egypt is one of dozens of countries with whom we are speaking about US technology leadership on artificial intelligence,” a State Department spokesperson said. American AI “benefits the world”, they added, and the US “stands ready to partner with countries on AI development and deployment in ways that respect sovereignty and expand capabilities”.
Washington has also told the world that using certain Huawei accelerators without its approval can carry a legal penalty. Whether officials have raised that with Cairo is not known.
AI chip shipments to Egypt have needed American permission since 2023, which gives the administration leverage through the licensing process. Egypt is one of about 40 countries in that category.
Malaysia is the precedent
Malaysia announced a national AI system running on Huawei chips last year, on a similar scale to the Egyptian proposal. It then distanced itself from the project once the White House raised concerns.
“Malaysia remains committed to full compliance with all applicable export control laws,” the country’s investment ministry said at the time. It also reaffirmed its “sovereign right to formulate its policies in line with national interest”.
Malaysian customs seized a $13m chip shipment bound for re-export in June.
Why Egypt
Egypt has more than 100 million people and has been deepening ties with China across trade and military exercises. Xi Jinping travels there next week, his first visit in more than a decade.
The country’s second national AI strategy targets a 7.7% contribution to GDP by 2030, and it does not make its own chips. That leaves the US or China.
American infrastructure companies have not historically treated Egypt as a market, and it has not been a priority for Trump’s AI diplomacy. Huawei has been present there for decades. It is courting African governments on education and healthcare, including in Kenya.
The wider chip fight
Trump’s team scrapped a Biden-era plan to widen the export curbs globally, partly to avoid handing markets to Huawei. An export promotion programme for Global South countries launched over a year ago and has produced no deals. The State Department pointed to it. It would not say whether federal money is available for Egypt.
Brazil is already building two AI supercomputers, one Chinese and one American. Chinese chipmakers have been moving to custom silicon under the same pressure, and Huawei won a $1.7bn China Telecom deal in June.
At home, DeepSeek and Moonshot still run on Nvidia hardware. One Huawei scientist has argued Nvidia will hit the same wall everyone else does.
What to watch
Egypt has not said which bid it prefers, and neither side has confirmed a decision date. Bloomberg notes the tender may be the first time the US and China have competed directly for one government AI project.
Xi arrives next week. Whether the US consortium exists by then is the open question, because nobody has confirmed that Nvidia, AMD or Microsoft agreed to join one.

report.summary: 华为竞标埃及AI数据中心，美国紧急组联盟对抗。
report.background: 华为在美国制裁下仍积极拓展海外AI芯片市场，此次竞标埃及政府AI数据中心，计划出口2008颗Ascend系列芯片，并与iFlytek合作提供监控技术。美国国务院随即联系英伟达、AMD和微软组建竞争联盟，并警告使用华为加速器可能面临法律惩罚。这是美中首次直接竞争单一政府AI项目，埃及拥有逾亿人口和2030年AI贡献GDP 7.7%的战略目标，但自身不产芯片，不得不在中美之间权衡。马来西亚此前因美国施压而疏远华为，为埃及提供了先例。
key_points: 华为首次确认出口Ascend 950系列高端芯片，数量不大但标志着其突破美国出口管制、进入海外AI基础设施市场的关键尝试。
华为与语音和监控公司iFlytek合作，提供车辆识别、个人识别及城市全景监控功能，引发西方对数据安全和隐私的担忧。
美国国务院紧急接触英伟达、AMD和微软寻求联合竞标，但尚无公司确认加入，同时以出口许可和法律责任为筹码施压埃及。
马来西亚先例显示，美国施压可让客户退缩，但埃及与中国关系深厚，习近平下周访问埃及使地缘博弈更显复杂。
这是中美首次在政府AI项目上正面竞争，结果可能重塑全球AI技术阵营和出口管制的实际边界。
report.impact: 对AI行业而言，全球供应链将进一步分裂为中美两套生态，企业面临选边站的压力。对开发者，未来或需在华为CANN/MindSpore与英伟达CUDA等不兼容工具链间做选择，跨生态开发成本上升。对普通用户，尤其是在发展中国家，AI技术普及可能伴随更大的政府监控风险，而美国方案也可能附加条件。总体来看，地缘政治正主导AI发展路径，技术中立性日益减弱。
report.tools: 建议关注华为昇腾生态（MindSpore、CANN）和英伟达/AMD开源工具（如CUDA、ROCm）以理解技术差异；跟踪国际出口管制动向可参考CSIS报告或Bloomberg科技板块。
